subject: Accounting
title: Evergrande's Debt Bomb
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Evergrande's Debt Bomb.

hook.text: China Evergrande had $300 billion in liabilities. Its accounting made the situation look manageable.

buildup.text: The property developer booked revenue from apartments before they were built or delivered.

discovery.text: Off-balance-sheet vehicles and related-party transactions obscured the true scale of debt.

twist.text: When China tightened rules, Evergrande couldn't refinance. The dominoes started falling.

climax.text: The default threatened China's financial system and wiped out billions in investor wealth.

punchline.text: Hidden debt doesn't vanish. It compounds.

quiz.question: How did Evergrande obscure its debt?
options: Off-balance-sheet vehicles and early revenue recognition

details.summary: China Evergrande became the world's most indebted property developer by aggressively borrowing to fuel rapid expansion. This topic covers how Evergrande hid the scale of its liabilities, the impact on the Chinese economy, and what it reveals about financial transparency.
details.whyItMatters: Evergrande illustrates how excessive leverage combined with opaque accounting can create systemic risk that threatens an entire economy, not just one company.
takeaways: Evergrande accumulated over $300 billion in liabilities while projecting financial health
Complex corporate structures and related-party transactions obscured the true debt picture
The default triggered a broader Chinese real estate crisis affecting millions of homebuyers

faq.question: What happened with China Evergrande?
faq.answer: Evergrande, China's largest property developer, accumulated over $300 billion in debt while aggressively expanding. When it could no longer service this debt in 2021, it triggered a credit crisis across China's real estate sector, affecting suppliers, banks, and millions of homebuyers.

faq.question: How did Evergrande hide its financial problems?
faq.answer: Evergrande used complex corporate structures, related-party transactions, and opaque off-balance-sheet arrangements to obscure the full extent of its liabilities. Pre-selling apartments generated cash but created massive delivery obligations not always transparent to investors.
